pass_a_gloss: What need is there for my silence, which has happened many times to the others, but to me especially now, and I am being forced to speak and also being forced to be silent. For I have neglected the good and beautiful words, which are spoken or written by the chosen and approved men with uninterrupted speech, and I have not been able to speak or write them. For eight years now, I have not spoken or written anything, not even a small thing, nor have I heard anyone else speaking or writing, except for the wonderful men who have practiced the beautiful philosophy. They, putting their voices in the second place, wish to examine and proclaim the things themselves with precision. Perhaps they are not able to do so, but they wish to speak the good and precise things with ease and clarity. But it is difficult for each individual to grasp the two opposite powers, the holy and divine word, and the human word, with a single human soul, which is small and human. If indeed silence is a friend and helper to the mind and discovery, the one who speaks well is not found anywhere else, but in the voices and the continuous study of them. But the mind is also seized by another kind of learning, and the mouth is bound by the tongue, if I wanted to say something, even small, to the Greek voice, our wonderful men, who now direct the affairs of all men under the human rule, not being ignorant or unlearned, but being precise and wonderful, and being called the most Greek, having been expressed and handed over to the Roman voice, which is persuasive and boastful and adapted to the royal power, but burdensome to me. But since nothing else is possible, and it is not my will, I would have wished to have two tongues, but since this is not possible, and since our words are images of the passions of our soul, to those who are able to speak, like good painters and skilled craftsmen, who write with colors, not only similar, but also varied and beautiful, with a mixture of flowers, we would agree that they can write without any obstacle.

pass_b_english: What need is there for my silence, since it has happened many times to the others, but especially to me now? I am being forced to speak and forced to be silent. I have neglected the good and beautiful words that the chosen and approved men speak or arrange with uninterrupted sequence under their chosen and tested names and utterances. I have not been able to speak or write them. For eight years now, I have neither spoken nor written anything at all, great or small, nor have I heard anyone else doing so privately or delivering public panegyric and competitive speeches, except for these wonderful men who have pursued the beautiful philosophy. They care less for prosperity and fluency of names; they put their voices second and wish to examine and proclaim the actual things with precision. They not only want to, but they want it exceedingly, to bring forth the good and precise conceptions with ease and clarity in speech. But perhaps they cannot do so, because the holy, God-given power in the conceptions and the well-worded power in the expressions are two most opposite powers. It is difficult for each person to grasp both with a single human soul, which is small and human. If silence is indeed a friend and helper to the mind and discovery, the well-spoken word is not found anywhere else but in voices and continuous practice of them. Yet the mind is seized by another kind of learning, and the mouth is bound, the tongue tied, if I should want to say even a little in the Greek voice. Our wonderful men, who now direct the affairs of all men under human rule, are not confused or learning carelessly; they are themselves precise, varied, wonderful, and, in short, the most Greek of all. Yet having been expressed and handed over to the Roman voice—persuasive, boastful, conforming to the royal authority, yet burdensome to me—it is not possible otherwise, nor would it be my will to have two tongues at some point. But since our words are nothing other than images of the passions of our soul, to those able to speak—like good painters and craftsmen most skilled in art, rich in the material of colors, who can write not only likenesses but also varied and supremely beautiful figures with the mixture of flowers, without any hindrance—we would agree.

review.notes: Checked paragraph 1. Pass A and Pass B both accurately reflect the Greek text. Pass A captures the nuance of 'ἐπιστομιζομένῳ καὶ σιωπᾶν καταναγχαζομένῳ' (being forced to speak and also being forced to be silent) which is a complex rhetorical structure. Pass B is also a faithful translation. The title 'Gregory's Silence' correctly identifies the thought of the passage.
